title: Hubble view of NGC 922
caption: The ring galaxy NGC 922, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 922 · constellation Fornax · about 150 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: An almost complete circle of bright pink nebulae runs around a spiral galaxy in this Hubble image of NGC 922. The pink ring and the galaxy's twisted spiral shape both trace back to a single event.

Some 330 million years ago, a smaller galaxy scored a direct hit, plunging right through the centre of NGC 922. A collision like this sends a disturbance rippling outward through the larger galaxy's disc, like a stone dropped into a pond, and it bends the galaxy out of its original form.

The pink colour marks nebulae, clouds of gas lit up by young stars. As the ripple moves outward, it compresses gas and sets off star formation, which is why the ring is lined with glowing clouds. Galaxies shaped this way are known as ring galaxies, and NGC 922 is a clear example of how they form.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.17 x 2.17 arcminutes) and distance (150 million light years), the frame spans roughly 95,000 × 95,000 light-years. Its light set out about 150 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, with visible and near-infrared filters plus one for glowing hydrogen. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
filters: 665 nm · Optical redshifted H-alpha + [N II] (Hubble WFC3)
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see this way without a telescope, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot detect.
